description: YOLO (Yesterday's Objects, Lasting Outcomes) is inspired by the legacy of NASA's space exploration missions. We aim to bring attention to the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments left behind on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Through research, technology, and creative storytelling, we seek to make their histories, discoveries, and scientific contributions engaging and accessible to the next generation of space enthusiasts. Because a mission ending doesn't mean its story ends.
summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive space exploration archive that brings the stories of nine historic space missions back into focus. From the Apollo lunar experiments and the Pioneer spacecraft venturing into deep space to the Mars rovers, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker, and InSight, the project explores missions whose journeys ended, whose signals faded, or whose spacecraft were left behind.

Through immersive storytelling, authentic NASA imagery, mission timelines, scientific discoveries, and archival information, users can explore what each mission achieved, why contact or operations ended, and what humanity learned from it.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming space mission data and historical records into an engaging, accessible experience that encourages curiosity and scientific exploration. It highlights an important idea: a mission does not lose its significance when it stops operating. The knowledge, discoveries, and technological progress it leaves behind continue to shape our understanding of the universe.

Some explorers go silent. Their discoveries never do.
details:
Project title: Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Stories We Left Behind

Live project: https://abandoned-but-not-forgotten-lake.vercel.app/

Summary: An interactive, narrated web experience that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to nine pieces of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors tune in to each machine’s “signal,” learn how it was built and what it discovered, and see where it is now.

What it does and how it works

The project opens like an incoming radio transmission. After a short introduction about the machines humanity has sent beyond Earth, a faint signal interrupts. The visitor tunes it in with a slider, then meets the explorer in plain language: what it is, where it is, when it flew and what its job was. Each story is told backwards. It starts with the final recorded evidence, such as the last signal received or the place the machine still rests, and then rewinds through the chapters: why we built it, how it was sent, what it discovered, and what came home to Earth.

Every screen carries one idea, one NASA image with its credit, and optional narration. Visitors tap or press a key to continue, so they read at their own pace. After each story, they return to a map of nine signals: Opportunity, Apollo 11 Eagle, Pioneer 10, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Surveyor 3, ALSEP, InSight, Kepler and NEAR Shoemaker. They choose what to explore next and earn a rank as they listen. Once they have heard every signal, a final message about knowledge outliving the machines that gathered it opens. Each story ends with links to real NASA and JPL footage and images.

The engineering is always connected to the science. A visitor sees how Opportunity’s wheels, cameras and instruments led to evidence that Mars once held water, or how Pioneer 10’s flyby of Jupiter helped engineers design later spacecraft.

Benefits

  • It gives retired and silent machines a story. Young people mostly hear about active missions.
  • It needs no prior knowledge of astronomy, no account and no download. It works on a phone or a laptop.
  • It teaches evidence over legend. The Opportunity story includes a “fact or story” moment about the famous line “My battery is low and it’s getting dark.” Visitors learn that the rover actually sent numbers about dust and battery power, and a reporter turned them into a poem.
  • It is accessible. Narration is also on screen, narration and music can be turned off separately, the whole experience works with a keyboard, images have alt text, and animation is reduced when a device asks for it.

Intended impact

I want students to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers without being asked to feel sorry for them. Each machine is a way into the people who built it and the questions they asked. A visitor should leave knowing the names of a few of these missions, understanding how a machine’s design produced the knowledge it brought home, and curious enough to open the NASA pages linked at the end of each story. The core message is: we may have left these machines behind, but we have not left their stories behind.

Tools, languages and software

  • React, Vite, JavaScript (JSX) and CSS, built as a static site with no backend
  • React Router for navigation
  • HTML Canvas for the drifting starfield, and SVG for the final constellation
  • Web Audio API for the original generated ambient music, the tuning static and soft chimes
  • Web Speech API for narration, with support for recorded voice files
  • Google Fonts: Cormorant Garamond and Inter
  • Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub for development [add: GitHub Copilot, if you used it]
  • Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini for drafting story structure and code. I reviewed everything against NASA sources.
  • Vercel for hosting
  • Data and media sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), the NASA Image and Video Library, the NASA/JPL Photojournal, and NASA and JPL mission pages
  • Hardware: a personal laptop and phone for development and testing

How it is creative

  • The radio-signal premise. Visitors do not browse a catalogue. They tune a signal and discover an artifact, which turns learning into discovery.
  • Stories told in reverse. Each one begins with the last piece of evidence and rewinds, so the question “how did it get here?” drives the story.
  • A different dimension of curiosity for each machine. Opportunity is the will to keep going, Pioneer 10 is the courage to go farther, and Apollo 11 Eagle is the part that stayed.
  • No invented voices. I did not use talking-robot narration or made-up quotes. The emotion comes from documented history, such as engineers sending more than a thousand recovery commands over eight months.
  • A media-literacy moment built into a famous myth.
  • Sound design. The original ambient score and soft chimes create a calm, reflective mood, and the finale draws the nine signals into a constellation.
  • A restrained editorial look with serif headings and thin rules, so older students and adults are not talked down to.

Factors I considered

  • Accuracy: content is drawn from NASA and NSSDCA material, each story lists its sources, and every image carries its NASA credit. Machine-perspective text and invented quotes were removed.
  • Audience: ages 11 and up, plus casual space fans. Early versions changed screens on a timer and were too fast to read, so I rebuilt the experience around tap-to-continue, with short sentences and one idea per screen.
  • Tone and feel: early drafts used harsh sounds and a stressful look. I rebuilt the interface to feel calm and welcoming.
  • Accessibility and access: a static site with no accounts and no runtime API calls, so it loads quickly on phones and modest connections.
  • Attribution and copyright: NASA media is credited, nothing implies NASA endorsement, and the music is original rather than taken from any film score.
  • Scope: I chose a complete, polished flow across the Moon, Mars and deep space rather than a long list of shallow entries, and designed the map so more stories can be added.
